c.tagline: Baltic Hanseatic jewel of amber, brick gables and Solidarity history.

taxi.fareNote: Licensed taxis are metered and reliable, but app rides (Uber, Bolt, FreeNow) usually work out cheaper and avoid haggling over airport or rank fares.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number; 997 reaches police and 999 the ambulance service directly.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Overpriced-drink scams in Old Town 'gentlemen's clubs' and summer pickpockets along Długi Targ.

hood_desc: Gdańsk's showpiece Hanseatic core — the Long Market and Długa street, Neptune's Fountain, Artus Court, St Mary's Church and the medieval Crane on the Motława; the must-see, most walkable base for first-timers.
A regenerated river island opposite the old town, now a strip of design hotels, waterfront restaurants and cocktail bars linked by footbridge to the Long Market; best for dining and going out.
A lively district about 5km northwest, well connected by tram and SKM train, full of students, cafes, the Galeria Bałtycka mall and good-value hotels; a practical, local-feeling base.
A leafy, village-like district in the northwest with the Cistercian Oliwa Cathedral and its famous organ, the 18th-century Oliwa Park and the university; quiet, green and family-friendly.
A seaside residential area on the Bay of Gdańsk near Brzeźno's sandy beach and pier and Jelitkowo, with promenades and beach hotels; calm and best for summer swimming.
lodging: Hotel Almond Business & SPA by Grano

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink.

transit.hours: Trams and buses run roughly 5am to 11pm, with a network of night buses (prefixed N); the SKM runs frequently by day and hourly overnight on the main Tricity line.
transit.note: Gdańsk has no metro; trams and buses cover the city while the SKM/PKM trains link it fast to Sopot, Gdynia and the airport across the Tricity conurbation.
transit.pay: City trams and buses use ZTM tickets bought from machines, kiosks, on board (contactless card) or via apps like jakdojade and mPay; a single-ride ticket is about 4.20 zł and a 24-hour ticket about 20 zł. The SKM Tricity train (Gdańsk–Sopot–Gdynia) uses separate SKM tickets validated before boarding; a combined 'Bilet Metropolitalny' covers ZTM + SKM.

ferry: Seasonal Motława/Bay water trams (Żegluga Gdańska) to Westerplatte, Sopot and Hel

transit.m: PKM/SKM train to Gdańsk Główny (about 30-35 min)

tip.r: ~10% at restaurants for good service; rounding up is common. State the total you're paying when handing over the money rather than leaving it on the table.

landmarks: Long Market and Neptune's Fountain (Długi Targ)
The heart of the Royal Route, this pastel-gabled square centers on a 1633 bronze Neptune, symbol of Gdańsk's maritime golden age.
St. Mary's Church (Bazylika Mariacka)
Reputedly the world's largest brick church, this Gothic giant holds 25,000 people and rewards a 400-step tower climb with sweeping Old Town views.
Żuraw (The Medieval Crane)
Europe's largest medieval port crane, a 15th-century wooden colossus over the Motława that once hoisted cargo and ship masts by human-powered treadwheels.
Długa Street and the Golden Gate
Gdańsk's showpiece promenade runs from the 1612 Golden Gate past merchant townhouses meticulously rebuilt from wartime rubble in Flemish Renaissance splendor.
Artus Court (Dwór Artusa)
This opulent merchants' meeting hall on Long Market dazzles with a 10-metre Renaissance tiled stove and centuries of Hanseatic swagger.
Mariacka Street
Gdańsk's most romantic lane, where gargoyle-fronted terraces and amber jewellery workshops evoke the patrician city that inspired Günter Grass.
European Solidarity Centre
A rust-steel museum at the shipyard gates where Lech Wałęsa's Solidarity movement began, powerfully chronicling the strikes that helped topple communism.
Museum of the Second World War
An architecturally striking tilted tower above immersive underground galleries presenting the war's devastation from the city where its first shots fell.
Westerplatte
The windswept peninsula where World War II began on 1 September 1939, its ruined barracks and towering monument a place of solemn pilgrimage.
Oliwa Cathedral
This serene monastery church in Oliwa park is famed for its 18th-century rococo organ, whose 7,800 pipes and moving angel figures star in daily recitals.

train.note: Gdańsk Główny is a handsome brick station right beside the old town. PKP Intercity's Pendolino services reach Warsaw in about 2h45 and Kraków in 5h30, and the SKM commuter line runs constantly to Sopot and Gdynia. International services to Berlin route via Poznań and take around 8 hours. Book on the Intercity site for the cheaper advance fares.

bus.note: Coaches use the terminal behind Gdańsk Główny station. FlixBus runs to Berlin in about 8 hours and to Kaliningrad, Vilnius and the Czech cities. Carry your passport for the non-Schengen crossings. Domestic buses are less useful than the trains on most Polish routes.

intl.to: Nynäshamn, near Stockholm (Sweden) - sails from Gdynia, ~30 min by SKM train, ~18 hr
Hel & Sopot (Poland) - seasonal cross-bay boats, May-Sep

ferry.note: The Baltic crossings to Sweden leave from Gdynia, half an hour up the coast by SKM train, rather than from Gdańsk itself - allow for that when booking. Both are overnight sailings carrying cars and foot passengers, and cabins are worth booking ahead in summer. The seasonal boats across the bay to the Hel peninsula are a pleasant alternative to the long road round.

half.name: Sopot
half.blurb: Baltic seaside resort town with Europe's longest wooden pier, adjoining Gdańsk along the Tricity coastline.

half.name: Malbork Castle
half.blurb: The world's largest brick castle, a former Teutonic Knights stronghold on the Nogat River east of Gdańsk.

half.name: Hel Peninsula
half.blurb: Narrow sandy spit stretching into the Baltic Sea, with fishing villages, beaches, and a seal sanctuary.
